Owl Song," so deservedly popular throughout the Fraternity.
The book might easily have been ready for distribution at this time were it
not for complications as to the copyrights of the two songs just men
tioned. Both Brother Harrington and Brother Bridgman have endeavored
to secure permission from Oliver Ditson & Co., the publishers, to use the
music for these songs, but after long negotiations have recently been in
formed that the present business policyof the publishers forbids the courtesy
formerly extended with respect to copyrights. The council still hope
that some arrangement may yet be made whereby the Fraternity may
secure the privilege of publishing in their new book these very desirable
songs with the accompanying music. The editor recommends that the
same cover and loose style of binding should be repeated in the new
edition, with possibly an equally light but better quality of paper. There
seems no reason why the book cannot go to press in season to be ready for
the opening of the next college year.
Constitutional Amendments. The amendment of Section 8, Article
VI, adopted by the Convention of 1906 (General Resolution No. 5), and
the amendment of Section 6, Article II, adopted by the Convention of
1907 (General Resolution No. 3) have been duly submitted to the Chapters
and no objection thereto has been reported from any Chapter. Under
the provisions of Article X of the Constitution the amendments are now
in force. In connection with the amendment ot Section 8, Article VI,
relating to the discipline of members, the attention of the Chapters is
called to General Resolution iVo. 6, of 1906, presenting an
appropriate
form of By-Law to secure due notice before expulsion. Under the
amendment of Section 6, Article II, the Council will hereafter be com

Recommendations. The Council would respectfully urge :
That all the Chapters strictly observe the provisions adopted by the
Convention of 1903 with respect to Masters of the Rolls. The impor

the Fraternity.
That in view ot the approaching Seventy-fifth Anniversary of the
founding of the Fraternity special effort be made for suitable celebration
of the event by all the Chapters and Alumni Associations.
The New Council. We invite a moment's consideration to a few;
facts indicating the progress of the Fraternity in the
thirty-nine years
since the constitution of 1869 was adopted. During that period there
have been thirty-six members of the Council and thirty-nine annual Con
ventions. The roll of the Fraternity has grown from 3,525 to 11,078. Nine
new Chapters have been added and two Chapters (Alplia and Owtegd) have
surrendered their charters. Four catalogues and flve editions of the songbook have been published and the Constitution has been handsomely
printed. The insignia of the Fi'aternity and of the Chapters have been
prepared and published. A uniform badge has been adopted and a
Fraternity jeweler appointed. New Chapter houses have been established
and are still building Members of .the Fraternity have attained deserved
distinction and eminence in every honorable and useful walk of life find
to-day the Fraternity in its seventy-fifth year is more vigorous and
flourishing than ever before in its history.

15
It is a matter of profound satisfaction that the four Pounders who
were members of the Class of '36 lived to enjoy the successful fruition of
their estrly inspiration, and three of them survived until after 1900. Dur
ing the past year suitable tablets to the memory of the seven Founders
have been installed in all the Chapters.
The best wish that the Council of Five can express to the Council ol
Ten is that they may always enjoy the same hearty support and co
operation of the active and retired members of the Fraternity that have
been so
freely accorded to theiv predecessors.
Respectfully submitted.

(APPENDIX E')
Communication from Brother Smiley
Berkeley, California, April, 18, 1908.
To the 68th Convention of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity:
Since March, 1905, I have lived under the eaves of the University of
California, going on and off the campus almost daily during these yearp.
Today the campus is a lonely place. Everybody has gone to Stanford
University to the Annual track meet. When the meet closes the Psi U's
will at once take trains going away, but what the other fraternity men
will do maybe read in to-day's Berkeley Reporter as follows:
"A large representation from the University of California will visit
Stanford to be present at the track meet. Many of this number will
spend the week-end there as guests at their fraternity homes or of friends
in that college.
The Stanford chapter of the fraternity has issued invitations
for a dance to be given in its fine new home in Palo Alto. With the
double attraction of the meet and dance, a large number of the �
fraternity men of the University of California will go to Stanford."
To the fraternity men whose fraternities are represented in both Uni
versities, this going back and forth is ot immense enjoyment and profit.
There are a dozen such occasions each year. There also are joint dinners
in San Francisco every season. Consider the impression upon San Fran
cisco of two chapters with their alumni i'n comparison with one chapter
and a few alumni holding any public function. The last S. F. dinner of
Psi U. was not even mentioned in any of the papers. At an initiation in
the East I have often met representatives of six to ten chapters. Here I
can see no undergraduate visiting the lonelj' Epsilon. If you will recall
the condition ol the Theta before the Delta was organized you will see the
present condition of the Epsilon. As Stanford is so near by, the isolation
of the E. is emphasized. I feel this in behalf of the boys here much more
than they seem to feel it for themselves. Besides, they seem diffident about
asking the Fraternity to remedy this disadvantage. lam writing with
out their knowledge, and because I love the Dear Old Psi U.
My own idea is that the Annual Convention should show its love for
the E. by taking the initiative towards helping the E. out of its aloneness
by appointing a Committee and requesting that Committee at the earliest
opportunity to arrange for a Chapter of Sir. T. at Stanford. This means
that as soon as that committee certifies to an Annual Convention that it
has a proper nucleus for a chapter the Fraternity will present it with a
